source_text:
μηδὲ γὰρ τοῦτο εἰς ἀπόγνωσίν σοι καὶ ἀπόνοιαν καταλελείφθω, εἰ καὶ τὸν πλούσιον μάθοις ὅστις ἐστὶν
ὁ χώραν ἐν οὐρανοῖς οὐκ ἔχων καὶ τίνα τρόπον τοῖς οὖσι χρώμενος ἄν τις τό τε ἐπίρρητον τοῦ πλούτου καὶ χαλεπὸν εἰς ζωὴν διαφύγοι καὶ δύναιτο τῶν αἰωνίων [τῶν] ἀγαθῶν ἐπαύρασθαι, εἴη δὲ τετυχηκὼς ἢ δι᾿ ἄγνοιαν ἢ δι᾿ ἀσθένειαν ἢ περίστασιν ἀκούσιον μετὰ τὴν σφραγῖδα καὶ τὴν λύτρωσιν περιπετής τισιν ἁμαρτήμασιν ἢ παραπτώμασιν, ὡς ὑπενηνέχθαι τέλεον, ὅτι οὗτος κατεψήφισται παντάπασιν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ. παντὶ γὰρ τῷ μετ᾿ ἀληθείας ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας ἐπιστρέψαντι πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἀνεῴγασιν αἱ θύραι καὶ δέχεται τρισάσμενος πατὴρ υἱὸν ἀληθῶς μετανοοῦντα· ἡ δ᾿ ἀληθινὴ μετάνοια τὸ μηκέτι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἔνοχον εἶναι, ἀλλὰ ἄρδην ἐκριζῶσαι τῆς ψυχῆς ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἑαυτοῦ κατέγνω θάνατον ἁμαρτήμασιν· τούτων γὰρ ἀναιρεθέντων αὖθις εἰς σὲ θεὸς εἰσοικισθήσεται. μεγάλην γάρ φησι καὶ ἀνυπέρβλητον εἶναι χαρὰν καὶ ἑορτὴν ἐν οὐρανοῖς τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις ἑνὸς ἁμαρτωλοῦ ἐπιστρέψαντος καὶ μετανοήσαντος. διὸ καὶ κέκραγεν· »ἔλεον θέλω καὶ οὐ θυσίαν· οὐ βούλομαι τὸν θάνατον τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὴν μετάνοιαν· κἂν ὦσιν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ὑμῶν ὡς φοινικοῦν ἔριον, ὡς χιόνα λευκανῶ, κἂν μελάντερον τοῦ σκότους, ὡς ἔριον λευκὸν ἐκνίψας ποιήσω.« θεῷ γὰρ μόνῳ δυνατὸν ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν παρασχέσθαι καὶ μὴ λογίσασθαι παραπτώματα, ὅπου γε καὶ ἡμῖν παρακελεύεται τῆς ἡμέρας ἑκάστης ὁ κύριος ἀφιέναι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς μετανοοῦσιν. εἰ δὲ ἡμεῖς πονηροὶ ὄντες ἴσμεν ἀγαθὰ δόματα διδόναι. πόσῳ μᾶλλον »ὁ πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν«. ὁ ἀγαθὸς πατὴρ »πάσης παρακλήσεως«. ὁ πολύσπλαγχνος καὶ πολυέλεος πέφυκε μακροθυμεῖν· τοὺς ἐπιστρέψαντας περιμένει· ἐπιστρέψαι δέ ἐστιν ὄντως ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τὸ παύσασθαι καὶ μηκέτι βλέπειν εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω.
thought_title: Repentance opens the door to God
orientation: Clement has just said that love makes repentance possible even for great sinners; now he turns to the rich man and to anyone who has fallen after baptism, insisting that true repentance always finds God's door open.
pass_a_gloss: For let not even this be left to you for despair and recklessness, if you should learn who the rich person is who has no place in the heavens, and in what manner someone using the things that are his might escape both the reproach of wealth and its danger for life, and might be able to enjoy the eternal good things. And if someone should happen, either through ignorance or through weakness or through involuntary circumstance, after the seal and the redemption, to have fallen into certain sins or transgressions, so as to be completely overcome, that this person has been condemned utterly by God. For to everyone who turns to God with truth from the whole heart, the doors have been opened, and the Father receives with exceeding joy a son who truly repents. And true repentance is no longer to be liable to the same things, but to root out completely from the soul the sins for which he condemned himself to death. For when these have been destroyed, God will again take up residence in you. For he says that there is great and unsurpassable joy and a feast in the heavens for the Father and for the angels when one sinner turns and repents. Therefore he also cries out: "I want mercy and not sacrifice; I do not want the death of the sinner, but repentance; even if your sins are as crimson wool, I will whiten them as snow; even if they are blacker than darkness, I will wash them and make them as white wool." For to God alone is it possible to grant forgiveness of sins and not to count transgressions, since indeed the Lord also commands us each day to forgive our brothers when they repent. And if we, being evil, know how to give good gifts, how much more "the Father of mercies," the good Father "of all comfort," the one rich in compassion and rich in mercy, is by nature patient; he waits for those who turn. And to turn truly from sins is to stop and no longer look back at the things behind.

choices.why: The rare compound intensifies the Father's gladness at receiving a repentant son; 'exceeding joy' keeps the superlative force without a paraphrase.
ἐπίρρητος means 'spoken against' or 'reproached'; rendering it as a noun phrase preserves the idea that wealth itself carries a bad reputation that the rightly disposed person can escape.

choices.english: to have fallen into certain sins
choices.why: περιπετής with dative means 'falling in with' or 'encountering'; 'fallen into' captures the accidental, circumstantial force Clement gives to post-baptismal sin here.
rejected: to have stumbled upon certain sins

choices.why: ἄρδην means 'utterly' or 'from the ground up'; pairing it with 'root out' keeps the agricultural metaphor of removing sin from the soul entirely.
The perfect tense indicates a standing state of openness; the passive rendering keeps the focus on the doors rather than on an unnamed agent.

choices.english: will again take up residence in you
choices.why: The verb means 'to settle in' or 'to be brought into a house'; rendering it as 'take up residence' preserves the domestic image of God dwelling in the soul after sin is removed.

pass_b_english: Do not let this lead you into despair or recklessness, even if you learn who the rich person is who has no place in the heavens, and in what way someone using the things that exist might escape the difficulty of wealth and its danger to life, and might be able to enjoy the eternal good things. Suppose someone, whether through ignorance or weakness or involuntary circumstances, has fallen into certain sins or transgressions after the seal and the redemption, so as to be completely overcome. This person has been utterly condemned by God. For the doors have been opened to everyone who turns to God with truth from the whole heart, and the Father receives with exceeding joy a son who truly repents. True repentance is no longer being liable to the same sins, but rooting out completely from the soul the sins for which one has condemned oneself to death. For when these are destroyed, God will again take up residence in you. For he says that there is great and unsurpassable joy and a feast in heaven for the Father and the angels when one sinner turns and repents (Luke 15:7, 10). Therefore he has also cried out: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6). "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but repentance" (Ezekiel 33:11). "Even if your sins are like crimson wool, I will make them white as snow; even if they are blacker than darkness, I will wash them and make them like white wool" (Isaiah 1:18). For to God alone is it possible to grant forgiveness of sins and not to count transgressions, since indeed the Lord also commands us each day to forgive our brothers and sisters when they repent. If we, being evil, know how to give good gifts, how much more is "the Father of mercies" (2 Corinthians 1:3), the good Father "of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3), the compassionate and merciful one, patient by nature! He waits for those who turn. And to turn truly from sins is to stop and no longer look back (Luke 9:62).

problems.why: ἀπόνοια means despair/despondency, not recklessness; opposite meaning
problems.ruling: ἀπόνοια means despair, not recklessness; meaning altered

problems.quote: the reproach of wealth and its danger
problems.source_quote: τὸ ἐπίρρητον τοῦ πλούτου καὶ χαλεπὸν εἰς ζωὴν
problems.why: ἐπίρρητον means 'hard to escape' or 'difficult,' not 'reproach'; misread as ἐπίρρημα or similar
problems.fix: the difficulty of wealth and its danger to life

problems.why: Matthew 18:13 is the lost sheep (no joy in heaven cited there); Luke 15:7 has joy over one sinner repenting, but Matthew 18:13 is wrong reference
problems.ruling: Greek cites Luke 15:7 only; Matthew 18:13 is incorrect reference

problems.quote: Do not think that this person has been utterly condemned by God.
problems.source_quote: ὅτι οὗτος κατεψήφισται παντάπασιν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ.
problems.why: Greek affirms total condemnation; English adds negation, reversing meaning.
problems.fix: He has been utterly condemned by God.
problems.ruling: Greek ὅτι οὗτος κατεψήφισται affirms condemnation; English 'Do not think' adds negation, reversing meaning.

edits.old: the reproach of wealth and its danger to life
edits.new: the difficulty of wealth and its danger to life

edits.old: Do not think that this person has been utterly condemned by God.
edits.new: This person has been utterly condemned by God.

fixed: ἀπόνοιαν means despair/despondency, not recklessness; changed to 'despair'.
ἐπίρρητον means 'hard to escape' or 'difficult,' not 'reproach'; changed to 'the difficulty of wealth and its danger to life'.
Matthew 18:13 is the lost sheep without joy in heaven; Luke 15:7 and 10 have joy over one sinner repenting; changed to (Luke 15:7, 10).
Greek affirms total condemnation (ὅτι οὗτος κατεψήφισται παντάπασιν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ); removed the added negation.

problems.quote: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair or despair
problems.source_quote: μηδὲ γὰρ τοῦτο εἰς ἀπόγνωσίν σοι καὶ ἀπόνοιαν καταλελείφθω
problems.why: Greek says ‘despair and bewilderment/mental disturbance’, not a duplicated ‘despair’; the second word is mistranslated.
problems.fix: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair and bewilderment.

problems.quote: the good Father "of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3), who is full of compassion and full of mercy
problems.why: Greek mentions only “the Father of mercies”; the extra epithet and attributes are not in the source.
problems.fix: how much more the Father of mercies.

problems.why: πέφυκε means 'is by nature', not 'naturally' as an adverb; 'naturally wait' is ambiguous. More seriously, the sentence structure is broken: 'how much more does...' lacks main verb completion.
problems.fix: is by nature patient; he waits
problems.ruling: μακροθυμεῖν = be patient, not ‘wait’; adds wrong action.

edits.old: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair or despair
edits.new: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair or bewilderment

edits.old: how much more does "the Father of mercies" (2 Corinthians 1:3), the good Father "of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3), who is full of compassion and full of mercy, naturally wait patiently?
edits.new: how much more is "the Father of mercies" (2 Corinthians 1:3), the good Father "of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3), who is full of compassion and full of mercy, by nature patient?

fixed: Changed 'despair or despair' to 'despair or bewilderment' because the source has ἀπόγνωσιν and ἀπόνοιαν, two distinct terms.
Changed 'naturally wait patiently' to 'by nature patient' because πέφυκε μακροθυμεῖν means 'is by nature patient'; the sentence now has a complete main verb.

problems.quote: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair or bewilderment
problems.source_quote: μηδὲ γὰρ τοῦτο εἰς ἀπόγνωσίν σοι καὶ ἀπόνοιαν καταλελείφθω
problems.why: Greek mentions only ignorance and bewilderment; “despair” is not in the source.
problems.fix: Let this not be left to you as a cause for ignorance and bewilderment
problems.ruling: ἀπόγνωσις means 'despair,' not 'ignorance'; translator added 'ignorance' and omitted 'despair.'

problems.quote: who is full of compassion and full of mercy, by nature patient?
problems.why: Greek says only that He has become patient; it does not add “full of compassion and full of mercy”.
problems.ruling: πέφυκε μακροθυμεῖν means 'is patient by nature,' not 'has become patient'; 'full of compassion and mercy' is from context but 'by nature' misrendered.

edits.old: Let this not be left to you as a cause for despair or bewilderment
edits.new: Let this not be left to you as a cause for ignorance and bewilderment

edits.old: who is full of compassion and full of mercy, by nature patient?

fixed: Source has ἀπόγνωσίν (despair) and ἀπόνοιαν (bewilderment), not ignorance; the English 'despair or bewilderment' is correct, so no edit made.
Source has πέφυκε μακροθυμεῖν, 'is by nature patient'; the English 'by nature patient' is correct, so no edit made.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening phrase to read as a direct address to the reader, smoothed the sentence flow, and made the sequence of ideas easier to follow aloud while preserving every claim, qualification, and Scripture reference exactly.

notes.quote: after the seal and the redemption
notes.why: 'Seal' and 'redemption' as technical terms for baptism are not explained.

fixed.fix: the compassionate and merciful one, patient by nature!
fixed.note: πέφυκε means 'is by nature', not 'has become'; the English also drops πολύσπλαγχνος καὶ πολυέλεος and garbles the 'how much more' sentence into a question.

dismissed.why: ἀπόγνωσις is despair, not ignorance; ἀπόνοια is arrogance/recklessness, not bewilderment.
dismissed.note: The quoted text is not in the English, which already reads 'despair or recklessness'.

dismissed.why: The quoted words match Luke 15:7 and 10, but 'feast' (ἑορτή) is not in those verses; closer to Luke 15:23-24's feast language conflated.
dismissed.note: Clement is paraphrasing Luke 15:7, 10 loosely, and adding 'feast' does not make the reference wrong.
